To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
NK‐2 receptor activation of AA mobilization in CHO cells is critically dependent upon Ca2+ influx, and PKCα activation.
NK‐2 receptor stimulation leads to the activation of two distinct G‐protein‐coupled pathways which converge to release AA.
NK‐2 receptor activation stimulates Ca2+ influx, PKCα activation and arachidonic release.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the cloning of a cDNA encoding a human ileal NK‐2 receptor which, when transfected into CHO cells, mediates powerful neuro‐kinin‐A stimulated arachidonic‐acid and prostaglandins release.
the cloning of the human NK‐ 2 receptor cDNA, the characterization of its signal transduction properties and its potential role in human disease.
the cloning and functional characterization of the human NK‐1 and NK‐2 receptors and the elucidation of the signal transduction mechanisms underlying their actions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
NK‐2 receptor activation of Ca2+ influx, PKCa activation, and arachidonic release is a Gq‐mediated event, while the receptor‐dependent activation by NKA of phospholipase A2 is a Gi‐mediated event.
the NK‐2 receptor, when expressed in CHO, is linked to the mobilization of AA and PGs by a Ca2+-dependent pathway which is dependent upon the activation of PKCα.

NK‐2 receptor activation of the PKCα pathway and subsequent mobilization of AA is dependent upon Ca2+ influx, but not release from internal stores and that this Ca2+ influx may be mediated by more than one G‐protein.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the NK‐2 receptor is coupled via Gq/11 to phospholipase Cβ activation and to Ca2+ influx, but via Gi to PKCa activation.
the human NK‐ 2 receptor is a G‐protein coupled receptor that activates two major signal transduction pathways, one involving PKCa translocation and Ca2+ mobilisation and the other, Ca2+ influx.
the NK‐2 receptor can activate two major signal transduction pathways, one of which involves Ca2+ influx, the second PKC.
The main takeaway from our work is that
AA release by NKA is mediated through a Ca2+ influx‐dependent PKCα activation pathway.
NK‐2 receptors expressed in CHO cells are capable of mobilizing AA and this is mediated through a PKC‐dependent mechanism.
the NK‐2 receptor is a potent stimulator of AA release from CHO cells and that this response is critically dependent upon extracellular Ca2+, PKCα and G‐proteins.
